---
title: "Get Started"
engine: markdown
---

## Installation

```bash
quarto add jeroenjanssens/quarto-term
```

On first render, the correct binary for your platform is automatically downloaded from GitHub Releases and cached locally. Supported platforms: macOS (ARM and Intel), Linux (x86_64 and ARM), and Windows.

To build from source instead (requires [Rust](https://rustup.rs/)):

```bash
cargo build --release
```

## Your first document

Create a file called `hello.qmd`:

````markdown
---
title: "Hello Terminal"
format: html
engine: markdown
extensions:
  term:
    shell: zsh
---

```{term}
echo 'Hello, world!'
```

```{term}
for i in 1 2 3; do
  echo "Item $i"
done
```

```{term}
sleep 100 #! expect-prompt: false
ctrl-c #! literal: false, delay: 0.5
```
````

Render it:

```bash
quarto render hello.qmd
```

Here's how the rendered output looks:

```{term}
echo 'Hello, world!'
```

```{term}
for i in 1 2 3; do
  echo "Item $i"
done
```

```{term}
sleep 100 #! expect-prompt: false
ctrl-c #! literal: false, delay: 0.5
```

The `engine: markdown` line tells Quarto to skip its built-in execution engines. The `extensions: term:` key holds all configuration.

## How it works

1. The Lua filter collects all `` ```{term} `` cells from your document.
2. It sends them to the `quarto-term` binary, which spawns a persistent shell.
3. Each line is typed into the shell (simulating a real user), and output is captured via a terminal emulator.
4. The rendered output (with ANSI colors, prompts, etc.) replaces the original code cells in the document.

Because the shell session persists, variables, the working directory, and all other state carry over between cells.

## What it captures

Multi-line constructs like loops work automatically — the shell's PS2 continuation prompt (`>`) is detected and lines are grouped together:

```{term}
for planet in Mercury Venus Earth Mars; do
  echo "- $planet"
done
```

ANSI colors render faithfully, so colored output from compilers, linters, and CLI tools looks just like it does in your terminal:

```{term}
printf '\033[1;31mError:\033[0m file not found\n'
printf '\033[1;33mWarning:\033[0m deprecated API\n'
printf '\033[1;32mSuccess:\033[0m all tests passed\n'
```

Multi-line pipes work naturally:

```{term}
seq 1 5 |
paste -sd+ |
bc
```

## Configuration

All configuration goes under `extensions: term:` in your YAML front matter:

```yaml
extensions:
  term:
    shell: zsh
    spacing: true
    timeout: 15.0
    style:
      colorscheme: solarized-dark
```

See the [Reference](reference.qmd) for the full list of options, [Styling](styling.qmd) for colorschemes and fonts, and [Recipes](recipes.qmd) for common patterns.

## Using in a website or book

For standalone `.qmd` files, the filter is discovered automatically. In a Quarto project (website or book), you need to explicitly declare the filter in your `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

filters:
  - term

extensions:
  term:
    shell: zsh
    style:
      colorscheme: solarized-dark
```

Pages with only terminal cells still need `engine: markdown` in their front matter, or use ```` ```{.term} ```` (see [Using with knitr or Jupyter](#using-with-knitr-or-jupyter)).

## Using in a presentation

quarto-term works in RevealJS presentations. Terminal cells render on each slide with full ANSI color support and persistent state across slides.

```yaml
---
title: "My Presentation"
format: revealjs
engine: markdown
extensions:
  term:
    shell: zsh
    style:
      colorscheme: catppuccin-mocha
      cols: 64
---
```

Use smaller `cols` (e.g., 64) and optionally a smaller `font-size` to fit terminal output on slides. Here's a live demo:

```{=html}
<iframe class="slide-deck" src="demo-presentation.html" style="width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16/9; border: 1px solid var(--bs-border-color); border-radius: 6px;"></iframe>
```

## Using with other output formats

quarto-term supports all major Quarto output formats. Use format-specific style overrides to tailor the terminal appearance:

```yaml
extensions:
  term:
    style:
      colorscheme: dracula
      typst:
        font-family: "Fira Code"
        font-size: 9pt
      docx:
        font-family: "Consolas"
        font-size: 10pt
```

For **PDF via Typst**, use `format: typst` in your document — terminal output renders as styled monospace blocks with full ANSI color support.

For **Word** (`format: docx`), terminal output renders as a monospace table with background color, font styling, and ANSI colors.

For **EPUB**, the HTML renderer is used automatically — all styling works as in HTML.

See the [Reference](reference.qmd#output-formats) for the complete format support matrix and [Styling](styling.qmd#format-specific-overrides) for override examples.

## Using with knitr or Jupyter

Terminal cells can be written as ```` ```{term} ```` or ```` ```{.term} ````; both are the same to quarto-term. The difference is how Quarto's engines treat them:

| Page | ```` ```{term} ```` | ```` ```{.term} ```` |
|---|---|---|
| Only terminal cells | Needs `engine: markdown` (otherwise Quarto picks Jupyter) | Works as is |
| With `{python}` cells (Jupyter) | Works | Works |
| With `{r}` cells (knitr) | Doesn't work: knitr consumes the chunks, so cell options are lost and `include: false` chunks never run | Works |

So for pages with R code, write terminal cells as ```` ```{.term} ````; knitr leaves those alone. quarto-term warns when it finds ```` ```{term} ```` chunks that knitr has processed.

Terminal cells always run after all Python or R cells have finished: the terminal session runs during the Pandoc filter phase, not during engine execution. Terminal cells can use files that Python or R cells created, but not the other way around. With [Docker](docker.qmd), Python and R run on the host and terminal cells in the container, so they only share files through volumes.
